summary: An April Fools’ Day informational RFC (1 April 2019) from the Independent Stream. It satirically proposes four DNS record types, PASSWORD, CREDITCARD, SSN and SSNPTR, for storing customer data in public DNS. It is a joke about exposing sensitive information, not a real proposal.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a joke. It pretends you could write people’s secrets, like passwords and card numbers, in the internet’s public phone book. That would be a terrible idea, which is the point.

subtitle: Four joke DNS record types for storing customer secrets in the public internet phone book.

tldr.problem: Internet service providers need to manage customer data, but how do you share sensitive information like passwords and billing details across networks?
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8567 proposes storing this data in four new DNS record types: PASSWORD, CREDITCARD, SSN, and SSNPTR, making everything searchable and publicly accessible.
tldr.outcome: This April Fools RFC exposes the absurdity of treating DNS as a general-purpose data storage system. No legitimate system implements it.
tldr.outcomeLabel: A joke with a sharp point

today: RFC 8567 is an April Fools RFC from 2019, published for informational purposes only. It has never been implemented and is not used on the public internet.

sections.title: The Joke Setup
sections.content:
This April Fools RFC proposes using the Domain Name System (DNS) to store and share sensitive customer information across Internet Service Providers (ISPs). The RFC argues that because customers have weak network management, ISPs should treat CPE (Customer Premises Equipment) as a shared global responsibility and use DNS as a central repository for customer data.

The tongue-in-cheek framing cites real DNS extensibility (how the system has grown to support encryption keys, SSH fingerprints, and TLS certificates) to justify adding support for even more sensitive information.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS is like the internet's phone book. This joke says we should put everyone's passwords and credit card numbers in the public phone book so internet companies can share customer information.

sections.title: The Four Record Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines four new resource record (RR) types:

PASSWORD: stores a username and password pair, with passwords limited to 32 bits. CREDITCARD: holds a 16-digit card number, expiration date, and a Luhn checksum for validation. SSN: maps hostnames to US Social Security numbers and birth dates as 32-bit and 64-bit fields. SSNPTR: provides the reverse lookup, mapping Social Security numbers back to hostnames, enabling census-like queries across all subscribers of an ISP.

The RFC treats these with entirely straight technical descriptions: field formats, bit layouts, data types and algorithms like Luhn validation all receive serious specification.
sections.plainLanguage: It describes exactly how to store passwords, card numbers, and Social Security numbers in DNS, with careful bit-for-bit specifications, as if it were a serious proposal.

sections.title: The Sarcastic Security Argument
sections.content:
The security section notes that DNSSEC should be used to protect these records, ensuring the data originates from an authoritative source. This framing is the joke itself: the RFC presents the problem of malicious attackers providing false login credentials to DNS queries as something DNSSEC can solve, ignoring the fact that publishing real credentials in the public DNS is the actual security disaster.

The RFC also suggests that the SSNPTR RR enables population census functions and determining which family members live behind the same IP address by querying SSNs, treating privacy invasions as administrative conveniences.
sections.plainLanguage: It seriously suggests using security encryption on the DNS records, missing the point that putting secrets in a public database is the real problem, not whether it is encrypted.

sections.title: Why It Matters
sections.content:
RFC 8567 satirizes the tendency to repurpose DNS for purposes far removed from name resolution. The RFC acknowledges that DNS has already been extended with KEY, SRV, NAPTR, SSHFP, CERT, TLSA, CAA, and EUI records, each layering more functionality on a system designed for a different job. By pushing this pattern to its logical absurdity—storing passwords and Social Security numbers publicly—the RFC illustrates how easy it is to misuse a widely deployed infrastructure.

Published as informational, it is not a standard and was never intended to be implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: It shows how internet systems keep getting used for things they were never meant for, and what happens if you keep going: everything becomes searchable in a public phone book.
